There are mainly two types of branch instructions:

  1. Unconditional Branch: This always causes the program to jump to a specified address. Example: JMP 2050 (jump to memory location 2050).

  2. Conditional Branch: This occurs only if a specific condition is met, such as a zero result, negative result, or carry flag being set. Example: JZ 3050 (jump if zero flag is set).
    These instructions help control the flow of execution based on program logic and outcomes of computations.
sq.QUESTION_DESC: List and briefly explain two types of branch instructions.

sq.ANSWER: A branch instruction directly modifies the value of the Program Counter (PC). Normally, the PC increments by one after executing an instruction, moving to the next in sequence. However, when a branch instruction is executed, the PC is loaded with a new address, which may be specified in the instruction. This causes the CPU to jump to a new part of the program. In a conditional branch, the change occurs only if the specified condition is true. This application allows the CPU to repeat sections of code (loops) or make decisions (if-else).

Let’s consider the execution of an arithmetic instruction: R1 = R2 + R3. In a processor with three-bus architecture, the instruction is executed efficiently using internal buses A, B, and C.

Step-by-Step Execution Using Multiple Buses:

  1. Operand Fetch:

    • The control unit selects R2 and R3.

    • R2 is loaded onto Bus A, and R3 is loaded onto Bus B.

    • These are simultaneously fed into the ALU inputs.

  2. ALU Execution:

    • The ALU performs the addition of inputs from Bus A and Bus B.

    • The result is placed on Bus C.

  3. Write Back:

    • The value from Bus C is written into R1 via the register file's write port.

Efficiency Benefits in This Case:

  • All three operations—reading two operands, executing, and writing the result—can occur within one clock cycle, due to non-conflicting use of buses.

  • If only one bus were available, the operations would require at least three separate cycles.

This example demonstrates how multiple bus organization enables efficient execution of arithmetic instructions by facilitating parallel access and minimizing instruction latency.
